[[File:Foxtail millet (Setaria italica).jpg|thumb|Foxtail millet (''Setaria italica'') seeds, India.]]
'''Foxtail millet''', [[scientific name]] '''''Setaria italica''''' (synonym ''Panicum italicum'' L.), is an annual grass grown for human food. It is the second-most widely planted species of [[millet]] and the most grown millet species in Asia. The oldest evidence of foxtail millet cultivation was found along the ancient course of the [[Yellow River]] in [[Cishan culture|Cishan, China]], [[carbon date]]d to be from around 8,000 years before present.

Other names for the species include '''dwarf setaria''', '''foxtail bristle-grass''', '''giant setaria''', '''green foxtail''', '''Italian millet''', '''German millet''', and '''Hungarian millet'''.<ref>{{GRIN | access-date=7 January 2014}}</ref><ref>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref>

==Description==
Foxtail millet is an [[annual plant|annual]] [[Poaceae|grass]] with slim, vertical, leafy stems which can reach a height of {{convert|120-200|cm|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}.

The seedhead is a dense, hairy [[panicle]] {{convert|5-30|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long.

The small seeds, around {{convert|2|mm|frac=32}} in diameter, are encased in a thin, papery hull which is easily removed in [[threshing]]. Seed color varies greatly between varieties.

== Cultivation ==

=== History and domestication ===
The [[crop wild relative|wild ancestor]] of foxtail millet has been securely identified as ''[[Setaria viridis]]'', which is [[interfertility|interfertile]] with foxtail millet; wild or [[weed]]y forms of foxtail millet also exist. The earliest evidence for foxtail millet cultivation outside of its native distribution is at [[Chengtoushan]] in the Middle Yangtze River region, dating to around 4000 BC.<ref name="Castillo 2010">{{cite book |last1=Castillo |first1=Cristina |title=50 Years of Archaeology in Southeast Asia |date=2010 |publisher=River Books |isbn=978-6167339023 |editor1-last=Bellina |editor1-first=Bérénice |chapter=Still too fragmentary and dependent upon chance? Advances in the study of early Southeast Asian archaeobotany}}</ref> In southern China, foxtail millet reached the [[Chengdu Plain]] ([[Baodun culture|Baodun]]) at around 2700 BC<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guedes |first1=Jade d'Alpoim |display-authors=etal |year=2013 |title=Site of Baodun yields earliest evidence for the spread of rice and foxtail millet agriculture to south-west China |journal=Antiquity |volume=87 |issue=337 |pages=758–771 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00049449 |s2cid=55279328}}</ref> and Guangxi (near the Vietnamese border) at around 3000 BC.<ref name="Castillo 2010" /> Foxtail millet also reached Taiwan (Nankuanli, [[Dapenkeng culture]]) at around 2800 BC<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bellwood |first1=Peter |author-link1=Peter Bellwood |date=2011 |title=The Checkered Prehistory of Rice Movement Southwards as a Domesticated Cereal—from the Yangzi to the Equator |journal=Rice |volume=4 |issue=93 |pages=93–103 |bibcode=2011Rice....4...93B |doi=10.1007/s12284-011-9068-9 |hdl=1885/58842 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free}}</ref> and the [[Tibetan Plateau]] ([[Karuo culture|Karuo]]) at around 3000 BC.<ref name="Castillo 2010" />

Foxtail millet likely reached Southeast Asia via multiple routes.<ref name="Castillo 2010" /> The earliest evidence for foxtail millet in Southeast Asia comes from various sites in the Khao Wong Prachan Valley in central Thailand, with the site at Non Pa Wai providing the earliest date with direct [[Radiocarbon dating#Accelerator mass spectrometry|AMS dating]] to around 2300 BC.<ref name="Castillo 2010" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Weber |first1=Steve |date=2010 |title=Rice or millets: early farming strategies in prehistoric central Thailand |journal=Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=79–88 |bibcode=2010ArAnS...2...79W |doi=10.1007/s12520-010-0030-3 |s2cid=140535295}}</ref>

The earliest evidence for foxtail millet in East Siberia comes from the archaeological site at Krounovka 1 in [[Primorsky Krai]], dating to around 3620–3370 BC.<ref name="DiaoJia2017" /><ref>{{cite journal |last=Kuzmin |first=Yaroslav V. |year=2013 |title=The beginnings of prehistoric agriculture in the Russian Far East: Current evidence and concepts |url=http://revije.ff.uni-lj.si/DocumentaPraehistorica/article/viewFile/40.1/793 |journal=Documenta Praehistorica |volume=40 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.4312/dp.40.1 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The earliest direct evidence for foxtail millet in Korea come from [[Dongsam-dong Shell Midden]], a [[Jeulmun pottery period|Jeulmun]] site in southern Korea, with a direct AMS date of around 3,360 BC.<ref name="DiaoJia2017" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crawford |first1=Gary W. |last2=Lee |first2=Gyoung-Ah |year=2015 |title=Agricultural origins in the Korean Peninsula |journal=Antiquity |volume=77 |issue=295 |pages=87–95 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00061378 |issn=0003-598X |s2cid=163060564}}</ref> In Japan, the earliest evidence for foxtail millet comes from the [[Jōmon period|Jōmon]] site at Usujiri in [[Hokkaido]], dating to around 4,000 [[Before Present|BP]].<ref name="DiaoJia2017" />

Foxtail millet arrived in Europe later; carbonized seeds first appear in the [[second millennium BC]] in central Europe. The earliest definite evidence for its cultivation in the Near East is at the [[Iron Age]] levels at [[Tille Hoyuk]] in [[Turkey]], with an uncorrected [[radiocarbon]] date of about 600 BC.<ref name="zohary-hopf" />

=== Modern cultivation ===
In India, foxtail millet is still an important crop in its arid and semi-arid regions.<ref name="DiaoJia2017" /> In South India, it has been a staple diet among people for a long time from the [[Sangam period]]. It is referred to often in old [[Tamil language|Tamil]] texts and is commonly associated with Lord [[Muruga]] and his consort [[Valli]]. 

In [[Karbi Anglong district]] of Assam, India, millets have been an integral part of the food system of the Karbis as well as the [[Jhum]] fields. Hanjangmilen, Karbi name of foxtail millets have been visible in the Jhum fields in the past. But today it is hardly visible in the Jhum fields. But farmers are now bringing the traditional crop back into their food system which needs little water, grows well on poor soil, is fast-growing and suffers from very few diseases.

In China, foxtail millet was the main [[staple food]] in the north before the [[Song dynasty]], when wheat started to become the main staple food. It is still the most common millet and one of the main food crops in the dry northern part of the country, especially among the poor. In Southeast Asia, foxtail millet is commonly cultivated in its dry, upland regions.<ref name="Castillo 2010" /> In Europe and North America it is planted at a moderate scale for [[hay]] and [[silage]], and to a more limited extent for [[birdseed]].

In the northern [[Philippines]], foxtail millet was once an important staple crop, until its later replacement by wet-[[rice]] and [[Sweet_potato|sweet potato]] cultivation.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sheahan |first1=C.M |title=Plant guide for foxtail millet (''Setaria italica'') |url=https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/pg_seit.pdf |access-date=9 May 2017 |publisher=USDA-Natural Resources Conservation Service, Cape May Plant Materials Center}}</ref>

It is a warm season crop, typically planted in late spring. Harvest for [[hay]] or [[silage]] can be made in 65–70 days with a typical yield of {{convert|15,000–20,000|kg/ha|ST/acre}} of green matter or {{convert|3,000–4,000|kg/ha|ST/acre}} of hay. Harvest for [[cereal|grain]] is in 75–90 days with a typical yield of {{convert|800–900|kg/ha|ST/acre}} of grain. Its early maturity and efficient use of available water make it suitable for raising in dry areas.

=== Pests ===
Diseases of foxtail millet include leaf and head blast disease caused by ''[[Magnaporthe grisea]]'', [[smut (fungus)|smut]] disease caused by ''[[Ustilago crameri]]'', and green ear caused by ''[[Sclerospora graminicola]]''. The unharvested crop is also susceptible to attack by [[bird]]s and [[rodent]]s. Insect pests include ''[[Atherigona atripalpis]]'', the foxtail millet shoot fly.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780128042434/insect-pests-of-millets|title=Insect Pests of Millets: Systematics, Bionomics, and Management|year=2017|first1=A.|last1=Kalaisekar|first2=P.G.|last2=Padmaja|first3=V.R.|last3=Bhagwat|first4=J.V.|last4=Patil|publisher=[[Academic Press]] (AP)|isbn=978-0-12-804243-4}}</ref>

===Agronomic genetics===
